question: Norway is the largest supplier of pipeline natural gas to the EU. In the second quarter of 2026, it accounted for 51.2 % of the EU’s imports. The Norwegian Government has warned that, without the development of new fields, production will decline over the next decade, and is calling on the EU to reconsider its opposition to new oil and gas extraction projects in the Arctic.

However, on 21 September 2026, the Commission confirmed that it still stands by this opposition. At the same time, its Commissioner for Energy and Housing is warning of a price crisis linked to the supply crisis and is advising Member States to cut gas consumption. In light of the foregoing: 1.
Can the Commission explain where sufficient affordable gas is to come from in the future, given that it rejects Russian gas and, at the same time, rejects new projects by its largest supplier?
Does the Commission consider energy security to mean rejecting the expansion of European gas resources and then advising citizens and businesses to reduce their consumption?

In the event of a decline in Norwegian production, does the Commission have any alternative solution in place other than importing more expensive LNG from other parts of the world and then explaining to Europeans that they must cut down on their heating?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.11.2026) The Commission constantly works to ensure that Europe has and will continue to have a secure supply of energy, as a core function of the EU’s energy policy1. To that end, the Commission is in close and regular contact with all major global suppliers to ensure secure, diversified gas supplies to the EU, including Norway.

The global gas market is likely to be well supplied in the future. While the EU will still need fossil fuels from a diverse set of trusted partners during the transition, albeit in declining quantities in line with its clean energy transition, the ultimate objective is to limit dependency on fossil fuels, for both the climate and security.

Phasing out supplies from Russia, as part of the EU’s response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and end the EU’s strategic dependence on Russian energy, is a priority in that respect. It is not for the Commission to reject or approve European hydrocarbon extraction projects. Under the Hydrocarbons Licensing Directive2, which also applies in the European Economic Area3, this is a role for Member States.

The Commission is well aware of Norwegian government projections of declining hydrocarbon production4. As set out in the new EU Arctic Policy adopted on 20 October 20265, the Commission will work with partners to protect the Arctic environment and prevent all hydrocarbon reserve developments that threaten the Arctic ecosystem.

Through REPowerEU6, AccelerateEU7, the Electrification Action Plan8, the European Grids Package9, and many other efforts, the Commission continues its work of accelerating the transition to clean and affordable homegrown energy.
1 Treaty on the Functioning of the EU - Article 194(1)(b). 2 Directive 94/22/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May 1994 on the conditions for
granting and using authorizations for the prospection, exploration and production of hydrocarbons.

3 European Economic Area - Lex Factsheet 31994L0022 on Joint Committee Decision 019/1995 incorporating Directive 94/22/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May 1994 on the conditions for granting and using authorizations for the prospection, exploration and production of hydrocarbons into the EEA Agreement: https://www.efta.int/eea-lex/31994l0022.
